newsitem.title: UK: Businessman says was paid for predicting matches.
newsitem.headline: Businessman says was paid for predicting matches.

text.p: A Malaysian businessman accused of helping to fix soccer matches for a Far Eastern betting syndicate on Tuesday said he had received large amounts of money from Indonesia for predicting results.
The prosecution says Heng Suan Lim was sent more than 500,000 pounds ($802,00) from various Far Eastern sources which he used to pay off members of the match-fixing ring.

But Lim told a court that a wealthy Indonesian businessman called Johannes Josef had regularly sent him the money in exchange for inside information which would help him bet in the Far East on the results of English matches.
Lim also said he had spent much time in London casinos entertaining clients and estimated his total gambling losses at around 175,000 pounds.

Lim, along with former striker John Fashanu, is accused of paying one-time Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar to rig matches. The two men are also accused of running a similar scheme with former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers.
All four defendants deny the charges although Lim admitted he had helped the syndicate forecast matches with the help of insider information from Fashanu, Segers and Grobbelaar.
Lim also said Josef, a close family friend, had sent money to help him buy an apartment and would sometimes transfer cash even when no forecasts had been made.

"Mr Josef was my benefactor. Immaterial of whether there was soccer being played, he would give me money from time to time to build up my position," he told the court while being questioned by his lawyer Jerome Lynch.
But despite the closeness of his relationship with Josef and other friends in Malaysia, Lim declined to invite them to the trial to testify on his behalf.
"Considering the circumstances of the case I was sure they would be arrested immediately and I didn't want them to go through that," he said.

Lim met Fashanu in 1990 and soon the player was providing information to be passed onto Josef, who would typically bet a total of between 40,000 pounds and 50,000 pounds on the results of four or five English matches each weekend.
"Did you ever, ever talk to Fashanu about throwing matches?" Lynch asked.
"Not at all," replied Lim, who was asked to explain one payment of 17,000 pounds from Josef in May 1993.
"It must have been a good week before that. I must have had four out of four correct predictions," he said.
In November 1992 Fashanu introduced Lim to Grobbelaar, who seemed keen to earn money by helping forecast matches. But things did not go well at first and contacts dropped off.
"With due respect to Bruce, some of his November and December forecasts were a disaster. He felt a bit embarrassed to call me," said Lim.

The prosecution says Lim met Grobbelaar three times between September 1993 and February 1994 to hand over money for fixing games but Lim said the real reasons for the meetings -- one of which he denied took place -- were more mundane.

In early February 1994, the night before an away game at Norwich, Grobbelaar drove down to London to see Lim. The businessman said the goalkeeper had been depressed about the future of his career at Liverpool.
"He wasn't in good form. He was quite worried about his professional career. He was quite down and wanted some reassurances and things like that," Lim said.
Asked to explain regular payments of between 2,500 and 6,000 pounds he made to Fashanu in 1992 and 1993, Lim said he had been repaying money the player lent him to use in casinos.

"I lost in the region of 175,000 pounds. I am not proud of that," he said. "I did not go to casinos myself, but with guests. It sounds like a good excuse, but that's a good way of improving friendships and bonding."
